title: The 1962 rule that stops matches falling apart
description:
Pair 4 students with 4 schools at random and on average 3 student-school pairs would both rather have each other than what they got. David Gale and Lloyd Shapley's 1962 fix: every student applies to their top school, each school keeps its favourite on hold (a maybe, not a yes) and turns the rest down, and rejected students apply to their next choice until everyone has a place. Schools only ever trade up, so any school a student prefers has already turned them down for someone it liked more: no pair can break away. American hospitals had been matching doctors essentially this way since 1952, and Shapley shared the 2012 economics Nobel with Alvin Roth for this line of work.

Numbers checked in code: 100,000 random 4x4 setups (random pairing: 3.0 breakaway pairs on average; this rule: zero, every time). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gale%E2%80%93Shapley_algorithm

beats.say: Random matching: 3 breakaways. One rule: zero.
Not a smarter computer. Just a rule two mathematicians found in 1962.
You're matching students to schools. A breakaway is a student and a school who'd both rather have each other.
Step one: every student applies to their top school. Ana and Ben both pick Oak.
Each school keeps its favourite on hold. A maybe, not a yes. Oak holds Ben and turns Ana down.
Turned down? Try your next choice. Ana tries Elm, and Elm likes her more than Cy. Cy is bumped, tries Oak, no, then Fir. Done.
Bumping people sounds like trouble. It's the reason nobody breaks away.
Cy would rather have Elm or Oak. But Cy asked them first, and both said no for someone they liked more. Schools only ever trade up.
100,000 random setups: zero breakaways. Hospitals had been matching doctors this way since 1952.
So who comes out ahead: the side that asks, or the side that answers?
